title: Excessive disclosure of homeowner identity and household details during registration
description: During account registration and device enrollment, the homeowner may be prompted to provide more personal data than is necessary for initial setup, such as full identity, precise address, household composition, or unnecessary profile attributes. The privacy threat arises from the source sharing this data with the Home Hub.
assumptions: The registration/enrollment flow may collect account and device-binding information beyond the minimum needed to provision the hub and pair devices.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement for disclosure via oversharing/minimization issues; exact sub-node may differ in the project taxonomy.

title: Identification of the homeowner from registration traffic and device identifiers in transit
description: Data sent during registration and enrollment can contain direct identifiers (e.g., email, username) or indirectly identifying device serial numbers, MAC addresses, or installation metadata. If exposed on the flow, these can identify the homeowner or household.
assumptions: The flow carries account credentials/identifiers and device identifiers during setup, and transport protections may be absent, weak, or observable by intermediaries.
uncertainty_note: Exact identifying fields are inferred from typical registration/enrollment flows.

title: Linkability between homeowner account and enrolled devices via setup traffic
description: The enrollment flow can bind multiple cameras and sensors to the same account or hub using stable identifiers. Observing or reusing these identifiers can allow different devices and setup events to be linked to the same household.
assumptions: Enrollment transmits stable device identifiers and account/hub identifiers together or in a correlatable sequence.
uncertainty_note: Specific protocol details are not provided, so the degree of linkability depends on implementation.

title: Home Hub stores registration and enrollment data beyond what is necessary
description: On receipt of registration and device-enrollment data, the Home Hub may retain unnecessary personal data, raw identifiers, or detailed setup metadata, increasing exposure of homeowner and household information.
assumptions: The Home Hub persists account details, device identifiers, and setup metadata locally or forwards them for storage.
uncertainty_note: Retention behavior is not specified; threat applies if the hub stores more than needed or for too long.

title: Insufficient transparency about how registration and device data will be used
description: The Home Hub may not adequately inform the homeowner, at the point of registration and enrollment, what personal data is collected, which device metadata is stored, whether data is shared onward, and for what purposes. This leaves the homeowner unaware of processing.
assumptions: The setup interface may provide limited or unclear privacy notices during onboarding.
uncertainty_note: Applies if onboarding lacks clear just-in-time notice or understandable explanations.

title: Registration and enrollment proceed without valid or granular consent
description: The Home Hub may bundle account creation, device enrollment, telemetry, and optional data uses into a single acceptance step, preventing the homeowner from giving specific, informed, and freely given consent for distinct processing purposes.
assumptions: Some processing during setup may rely on consent or user agreement, and choices may be bundled or preselected.
uncertainty_note: Whether consent is the correct legal basis depends on context; if another basis applies, this may instead be a transparency/choice issue.

title: Homeowner cannot later prove or contest what was submitted during registration/enrollment
description: If the Home Hub does not provide receipts, confirmations, or auditable records of what account details and devices were enrolled, the homeowner may be unable to demonstrate what data was provided or dispute later claims about enrollment actions.
assumptions: The system may lack user-visible confirmation records or tamper-evident logs for onboarding actions.
uncertainty_note: Repudiation is less central here than disclosure/linkability, but can genuinely arise in account/device enrollment flows.

title: Temporary access code in transit can identify a specific guest session or guest user
description: The temporary access code transmitted from the Guest User to the Home Hub may act as a unique or near-unique identifier for a guest access session. Anyone able to observe the flow or its metadata could associate repeated uses of the same code with the same guest invitation or infer which guest is attempting entry.
assumptions: Assumes the code is observable on the communication path or via local interception, and that codes are unique per guest or per visit window.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-effort based on general LINDDUN identification taxonomy; exact node numbering may vary by version.

title: Observation of unlock-code submission reveals guest participation
description: Even without learning the code value, observing that this flow occurs can reveal that a guest is currently attempting to access the home. The mere existence and timing of the communication may disclose involvement or presence at the property.
assumptions: Assumes an attacker can observe network traffic, radio traffic, or visible interaction side-effects correlated with code entry.
uncertainty_note: Grounded in LINDDUN Detecting guidance from the provided context; exact tree node id is best-effort.

title: Home Hub can link guest code use across events
description: If the Home Hub stores or correlates temporary access codes, timestamps, and door-unlock events, it can link multiple access attempts to the same guest invitation or infer patterns about a guest's visits. This enables building a profile of guest presence over time.
assumptions: Assumes the Home Hub logs code submissions or successful/failed unlock attempts and retains them long enough for correlation.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree node id is best-effort; applicability depends on whether the hub logs and correlates guest-code events.

title: Guest may be unable to deny having used a temporary code if the Home Hub keeps attributable logs
description: If the Home Hub records the submitted temporary code together with timestamps and unlock outcomes, those records may later be used as evidence that a particular guest accessed or attempted to access the home. This creates a privacy risk where the guest cannot plausibly deny participation.
assumptions: Assumes temporary codes are attributable to a specific guest or invitation and that logs are retained.
uncertainty_note: This is a genuine privacy threat only if codes are attributable to an individual guest; otherwise applicability is weaker.

title: Guest may not be aware of logging and secondary use of temporary code submissions
description: The Home Hub may process the entered temporary code for purposes beyond immediate authentication, such as logging, analytics, alerting the homeowner, or retention for audit. If the guest is not informed about these purposes, retention periods, or recipients, they may lack sufficient awareness and control over processing.
assumptions: Assumes the system provides limited notice to guests about how temporary code submissions are processed.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort tree node id; this threat depends on the actual transparency and consent/notice mechanisms provided to guests.

title: Event records enable linkage of household activities over time
description: By writing motion, door, and other sensor events into a persistent local log, the Home Hub creates a longitudinal record that can be linked across timestamps and sensor types to reconstruct routines, occupancy patterns, and relationships between events within the same household.
assumptions: The local event log stores multiple events over time with timestamps or other correlators.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is best-effort based on generic LINDDUN linkage semantics; exact sub-node may differ in the canonical threat tree.

title: Sensor-event contents may identify residents or visitors indirectly
description: Even if the log does not contain explicit names, sequences of motion and door events written by the Home Hub can single out a household or identifiable individuals through distinctive behavioral patterns, presence schedules, or association with a specific dwelling.
assumptions: Events are associated with a particular home or device set and retained with sufficient granularity to distinguish patterns.
uncertainty_note: This is indirect identifiability from behavioral data rather than explicit identifiers; applicability depends on event granularity and context.

title: Local event log reveals sensitive inferences about behavior and occupancy
description: Once stored in the Local Event Log, motion, door, and sensor events can disclose when people are home, asleep, away, entering specific areas, or following particular routines. The destination data store therefore enables disclosure of sensitive personal information beyond the raw event values.
assumptions: The log is accessible to local administrators, support personnel, malware, or other components, or may later be queried/exported.
uncertainty_note: Exact disclosure sub-node may vary depending on whether the canonical tree distinguishes content disclosure from inference disclosure.

title: Persistent logging increases detectability of residents' activities
description: Storing sensor events in the Local Event Log makes otherwise ephemeral household activities detectable after the fact. Anyone with access to the log can determine whether motion or door activity occurred at specific times, making presence and actions observable.
assumptions: The log retains timestamps and can be accessed or inspected by some actor beyond the immediate sensing function.
uncertainty_note: Best-effort node selection for detectability due to persistence of event traces.

title: Logging may exceed users' expectations about purpose or retention
description: Residents may expect sensors to support immediate automation only, not long-term storage of detailed event histories. Writing all motion/door/sensor events to the Local Event Log can therefore create unawareness about what is stored, for how long, and for which secondary uses such as troubleshooting, analytics, or incident review.
assumptions: Users are not clearly informed about the existence, scope, retention, or uses of the local event log.
uncertainty_note: This threat depends on the surrounding notice and transparency mechanisms, which are not described in the flow.

title: Event logging may be non-compliant if excessive or retained without proper basis
description: The Local Event Log may store more granular household activity data than necessary, or retain it longer than justified, creating risk of non-compliance with data minimization, storage limitation, transparency, or lawful-basis obligations under applicable privacy requirements.
assumptions: Applicable privacy requirements govern household event data and the system lacks adequate minimization, retention limits, or notice/consent controls.
uncertainty_note: Compliance impact is jurisdiction- and implementation-dependent; exact legal obligation is not specified.

title: Excessive disclosure in uploaded camera clips
description: The Home Hub may upload full recorded clips containing more personal data than necessary for the storage purpose, such as bystanders, neighboring property, audio, or longer-than-needed footage. The act of sharing these clips to cloud storage creates a disclosure risk.
assumptions: Recorded clips can contain identifiable people, behaviors, timestamps, and contextual household information.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort based on general LINDDUN disclosure categories; exact sub-node may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Linkability via upload metadata
description: Metadata on the upload flow, such as device identifiers, account identifiers, IP address, timing, clip frequency, and file characteristics, can allow correlation of multiple uploads to the same household or user over time.
assumptions: Transport or application-layer metadata is observable or retained by intermediaries or the receiving service.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id may differ across LINDDUN Pro editions; classification as flow-level linkability is confident.

title: Identifiability from clip content and transmission metadata
description: The uploaded video clips and associated metadata may directly or indirectly identify residents, visitors, or the household through faces, voices, location cues, timestamps, device/account identifiers, or network information while in transit.
assumptions: Clips or metadata contain direct identifiers or strong quasi-identifiers.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is approximate; applicability of identifiability is strong.

title: Disclosure of sensitive footage in transit
description: If the upload channel is insufficiently protected or metadata is exposed, personal footage and associated information may be disclosed to unauthorized parties during transmission to cloud storage.
assumptions: Attackers, intermediaries, or service operators could access content or metadata if protections are weak or logging is excessive.
uncertainty_note: Assumes some realistic exposure path in transit; if strong end-to-end protections are in place, likelihood decreases.

title: Cross-clip and cross-device linkability in cloud storage
description: Cloud Video Storage can link uploaded clips across time, cameras, devices, or accounts using persistent identifiers, timestamps, and content features, enabling construction of detailed household activity patterns.
assumptions: The storage service maintains persistent identifiers and searchable metadata or analytics over stored clips.
uncertainty_note: Exact sub-node may vary; destination-side linkability is strongly applicable.

title: Identification of individuals by the cloud service
description: On receipt and storage, the cloud service may identify residents, visitors, or the household from video content, voice, surroundings, account data, or device metadata.
assumptions: The service has access to clip content and associated account/device metadata.
uncertainty_note: Tree node id is approximate; destination-side identifiability is strongly applicable.

title: Disclosure through cloud-side access or secondary use
description: Once stored, the cloud service may expose clips to unauthorized internal staff, third parties, law-enforcement requests beyond user expectations, or secondary uses such as analytics, causing disclosure of private household activities.
assumptions: Stored clips are accessible within the provider environment or shared under some operational or legal processes.
uncertainty_note: Secondary-use aspects can overlap with policy/compliance concerns, but disclosure risk at destination is genuine.

title: Unawareness of cloud retention and downstream use
description: Individuals captured in the clips, and possibly even the device owner, may be unaware that footage is uploaded to cloud storage, how long it is retained, who can access it, and for what further purposes it is processed.
assumptions: Notice and transparency about cloud upload, retention, and access are limited or not effectively communicated.
uncertainty_note: Exact node id may differ by version; destination-side unawareness is a strong fit.

title: Non-compliance with data minimization, retention, or lawful-basis obligations
description: Cloud storage of recorded camera clips may violate privacy obligations if the service stores more footage than necessary, retains it too long, lacks a valid legal basis or adequate notices, or processes footage incompatibly with the original purpose.
assumptions: Applicable privacy law or organizational policy imposes constraints on surveillance footage processing.
uncertainty_note: Compliance depends on jurisdiction and deployment context, but this is a plausible destination-side privacy threat.

title: Home Hub may disclose more motion-alert data than necessary to the backend
description: When forwarding a real-time motion alert, the Home Hub may include excessive personal data beyond what is needed for alert handling, such as precise timestamps, device identifiers, household identifiers, sensor metadata, or contextual details that reveal occupancy patterns. This creates avoidable disclosure to another party within the system.
assumptions: Assumes the motion alert contains or can be linked to household/user-related data and that some fields may be unnecessary for the backend's immediate alerting purpose.

title: Motion-alert transmissions may enable linkage of events to a specific household or user
description: Even if the payload is limited, repeated real-time motion-alert messages on this flow can carry stable identifiers or recognizable communication patterns that allow events to be linked to the same home, device, account, or resident over time. This can support profiling of occupancy and behavior.
assumptions: Assumes the flow includes stable identifiers, routing metadata, or persistent protocol-level identifiers observable within the system or by intermediaries.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is based on general LINDDUN linkage categories; exact sub-node may vary by the project's threat-tree version.

title: Real-time alert metadata may identify the household or resident
description: The content or metadata of the motion alert in transit may directly or indirectly identify a specific household, device owner, or resident, for example through account IDs, hub serial numbers, network addresses, or location-linked device identifiers.
assumptions: Assumes identifiers are present in payload or transport metadata and can be associated with a natural person or household.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id may differ across LINDDUN Pro versions; this is a best-fit identification-category node.

title: Motion-alert timing may reveal occupancy and behavior patterns
description: The frequency and timing of real-time motion alerts can reveal sensitive information about when people are home, awake, moving, or absent. Such detectability arises from observing the existence, timing, or volume of messages on the flow, even without full payload access.
assumptions: Assumes an observer or receiving infrastructure can observe message timing or volume.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node selection is a best-fit detectability node because the retrieved context did not include the detectability subtree.

title: Backend receipt and further exposure of motion alerts may exceed intended audience
description: On receipt, the mobile app backend may store, replicate, enrich, or make the motion alert accessible to additional internal services, operators, analytics components, or downstream processors beyond what is strictly required to deliver the alert. This increases exposure of personal data related to household activity.
assumptions: Assumes the backend persists or redistributes received alerts or associated metadata to other components or personnel.

title: Backend processing of motion alerts may be used for secondary purposes unknown to the user
description: The backend may process incoming motion alerts not only to deliver notifications but also for analytics, model training, service optimization, or other secondary purposes that are not transparent to the user. This creates an unawareness risk regarding how intimate in-home activity data is used.
assumptions: Assumes users are not clearly informed about all backend-side uses of motion-alert data.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is a best-fit unawareness node because the retrieved context did not include the unawareness subtree.

title: Backend handling of motion alerts may be non-compliant with data-minimization or purpose-limitation obligations
description: If the backend retains, enriches, or reuses motion-alert data beyond what is necessary for real-time notification, the processing may conflict with privacy obligations such as data minimization, storage limitation, purpose limitation, or transparency requirements.
assumptions: Assumes applicable privacy requirements govern household activity data and that backend practices may exceed the strictly necessary purpose.
uncertainty_note: Exact tree-node id is a best-fit non-compliance node because the retrieved context did not include the non-compliance subtree.

title: Notification content may disclose occupancy or in-home activity
description: By sending a motion-detected push notification, the backend shares personal information about activity at the home. If the notification text includes details such as motion time, camera/location, or event labels, it can disclose behavior patterns or presence/absence information to the homeowner's device and anyone able to view notifications there.
assumptions: Assumes the notification payload contains event details beyond a generic alert.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is best-effort based on generic disclosure-at-source semantics; exact sub-node may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Push-notification metadata can link homeowner, device, and home events
description: Even if notification content is minimized, the transmission of a motion alert can expose metadata such as recipient device token, timing, frequency, and association with a specific backend account. Observers or intermediaries involved in push delivery could use this to link repeated alerts to the same homeowner or household.
assumptions: Assumes standard mobile push infrastructure is used and metadata is visible to delivery intermediaries or network observers.
uncertainty_note: Exact linkage mechanism depends on push architecture and what metadata is exposed in transit.

title: Notification traffic may identify the homeowner or household
description: The push flow may carry identifiers or metadata that single out the homeowner's device or account, such as device tokens, account identifiers, or stable routing metadata. This can enable identification of the recipient or at least the specific household associated with the alerts.
assumptions: Assumes stable device/account identifiers are used in push delivery.
uncertainty_note: Identification may be indirect/pseudonymous rather than by real name, depending on implementation.

title: Notification preview on the phone may disclose private home activity to bystanders
description: When the homeowner's phone receives the motion-detected notification, lock-screen previews, wearable mirroring, or shared-device visibility can reveal sensitive information about activity at the home to people other than the intended recipient.
assumptions: Assumes notifications may be displayed on lock screen or mirrored to nearby/paired devices.
uncertainty_note: Tree node is approximate; the core issue is disclosure caused at the destination by local presentation of received data.

title: The homeowner may be unaware of notification visibility and downstream exposure
description: The recipient may not understand that motion alerts can appear on lock screens, wearables, notification histories, or cloud-synced devices, reducing their ability to control how this personal information is exposed after receipt.
assumptions: Assumes the app or platform does not clearly explain notification visibility settings and implications.
uncertainty_note: Usability/non-compliance boundary can vary; included here as an unawareness risk tied to receipt and presentation of the notification.

title: Sending detailed motion alerts without adequate user-configurable controls may violate data-minimization or privacy-expectation requirements
description: If the backend sends detailed motion notifications by default, without allowing the homeowner to choose generic versus detailed content or disable certain event categories, the sharing may exceed what is necessary and conflict with privacy expectations or applicable notification/privacy requirements.
assumptions: Assumes limited configurability or lack of explicit preference management for notification content.
uncertainty_note: Specific non-compliance depends on jurisdiction, product commitments, and implemented controls; tree node is approximate.

title: Backend shares analytics that may still be linkable to users or devices
description: Although described as aggregated device-usage analytics, the backend's act of disclosing analytics to the vendor can enable linking of records to the same user, device, household, or account if aggregation is coarse, persistent identifiers are retained, or small cohorts are shared.
assumptions: Assumes the shared analytics may include stable pseudonyms, device attributes, timestamps, cohort keys, or sufficiently granular segments.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context only confirms applicable threat types/positions, not detailed node ids.

title: Analytics transfer may reveal identifiable metadata in transit
description: Even if payload data is aggregated, the flow itself can expose identifying information through metadata such as source system, destination vendor, timing, tenant/account identifiers, API keys, IP addresses, or request headers, which may identify the organization or indirectly identify user populations.
assumptions: Assumes network- or protocol-level metadata is observable to intermediaries or logged by infrastructure.
uncertainty_note: Applies to flow metadata rather than payload contents; exact observability depends on transport protections and logging architecture.

title: Vendor can link received analytics with other datasets
description: On receipt, the cloud analytics vendor may combine the analytics with other customer data, telemetry, or third-party datasets, enabling cross-context linkage of cohorts, devices, or behavioral patterns beyond the original purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the vendor operates multi-tenant analytics services or has access to auxiliary datasets that make linkage feasible.
uncertainty_note: Specific linkage mechanisms depend on the vendor's platform design and contractual restrictions.

title: Vendor may infer sensitive behavior from aggregated usage analytics
description: Aggregated usage analytics can still disclose sensitive traits or behaviors about groups or, in small segments, about individuals—for example health, religion, location patterns, or vulnerable-status indicators inferred from app usage patterns.
assumptions: Assumes analytics dimensions are sufficiently granular or cohorts sufficiently small to support sensitive inference.
uncertainty_note: Whether this rises to individual disclosure depends on aggregation thresholds and segmentation granularity.

title: Secondary analytics use by vendor may exceed user expectations
description: The vendor may use the received analytics for purposes not expected by users, such as service improvement across customers, benchmarking, model training, profiling, or product development, making the processing insufficiently transparent and potentially incompatible with the original collection context.
assumptions: Assumes vendor terms or backend privacy notices do not clearly and specifically explain these downstream uses.
uncertainty_note: Classified as Unawareness because the key issue is lack of user visibility into downstream processing; could also overlap with non-compliance depending on stated notices and contracts.

title: Sharing aggregated analytics with vendor may lack a valid legal or contractual basis
description: Transferring analytics to an external vendor can violate privacy obligations if the data remains personal data or can be re-identified, and if appropriate controller/processor terms, cross-border safeguards, retention limits, or purpose limitations are missing or inadequate.
assumptions: Assumes the analytics may still qualify as personal data under applicable law or contract, and that governance controls may be incomplete.
uncertainty_note: Legal applicability depends on jurisdiction, anonymization robustness, and the actual vendor agreement.

title: Linkability via retrieval metadata on the video-transfer flow
description: When the backend retrieves a stored video clip from cloud storage, metadata on the flow (such as clip identifier, camera/device identifier, account/home identifier, timestamps, object path, request correlation IDs, or repeated access patterns) can allow events, devices, or household activities to be linked together beyond what is necessary for playback.
assumptions: Assumes the retrieval request/response or surrounding transport/application logs expose stable identifiers or rich metadata that can be correlated across requests.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is based on best judgement because the retrieved context did not include the specific Linkability subtree for DataStore->Process flows.

title: Identifiability of homeowner or household from video-transfer metadata
description: Even if the video content is protected, metadata carried on the retrieval flow may identify the homeowner or household, for example through account IDs, precise location-linked camera IDs, storage object names, or network-level identifiers associated with the request.
assumptions: Assumes identifiers tied to a natural person or household are present in protocol fields, URLs, headers, object names, or observably exposed logs/telemetry.
uncertainty_note: Specific Identifiability node citation is approximate; applicability depends on whether the flow exposes direct or indirect identifiers.

title: Backend learns more video content than necessary for playback delivery
description: On receipt of the clip, the mobile app backend may access, inspect, cache, or derive information from the full video content and associated metadata even when only minimal handling is needed to serve playback to the homeowner. This can disclose sensitive household activities, visitors, routines, or interior details to the backend processing environment.
assumptions: Assumes P2 terminates the retrieval and can access plaintext video or rich metadata rather than merely relaying opaque encrypted blobs.
uncertainty_note: Tree-node id is best-effort because the retrieved context did not provide the Disclosure subtree.

title: Backend can detect homeowner behavior from playback retrievals
description: By receiving video clips for playback, the backend can observe when a homeowner requests footage, which cameras are viewed, and how often or at what times playback occurs. These observations can reveal occupancy concerns, incidents, routines, or heightened monitoring behavior.
assumptions: Assumes P2 logs or can otherwise observe retrieval timing, clip selection, camera identifiers, or user/session context.
uncertainty_note: Specific Detectability node citation is approximate; threat is grounded in observability of access events at the destination.

title: Retrieved video is retained longer than necessary by the backend
description: After retrieving the stored clip, the backend may cache, log, or persist the video or derived metadata longer than needed for playback, violating storage-limitation obligations for personal data contained in home-security footage.
assumptions: Assumes P2 stores temporary copies, CDN/backend caches, debug artifacts, or access logs containing personal data without strict retention controls.
